newsitem.title: USA: N.Y Gov brushes off criticism of proposed tax cuts.
newsitem.headline: N.Y Gov brushes off criticism of proposed tax cuts.

text.p: New York Gov. George Pataki on Tuesday brushed off criticism by Moody's that he had proposed overly large tax cuts and Medicaid reductions in his 1998 fiscal budget.

"It's basically what we expected and I think Moody's ultimately will be more satisfied with the budget that we proposed than with the one the legislature ends up adopting," he told reporters in Albany.

The legislature likely would be tempted to raise spending, the Republican governor explained, adding he hoped the final budget that was adopted would let the state to make another contribution to the Rainy Day Fund, which got $65 million in fiscal 1997.

Bob Kurtter, a municipal analyst with Moody's Investors Service Inc, said earlier that the governor's proposed cuts in Medicaid were highly controversial, and pointed out they would be used to pay for most of the planned new tax reductions.

The Pataki Administration's fiscal 1998 budget assumes the legislature will follow through with a $700 million cutback in Medicaid planned for fiscal 1997, and top it off with another $900 million of cost containment efforts, Kurtter said, in prepared comments.

The tax cuts Pataki has proposed include property tax reforms to aid school districts, which will cost $1.7 billion when fully enacted over four years, another $1.7 billion of school aid, and reductions in estate and gift taxes.

Pataki's budget does not include a plan to eliminate the state sales tax on clothing that costs less than $500 -- a step Moody's said could cut state revenues by $600 million to $700 million -- though Assembly Speaker Sheldon Silver, D-Manhattan, and New York City Mayor Rudolph Giuliani both back the idea.
A report on the state's one-week moratorium on its four percent sales tax, which was matched by many cities and counties, including New York City, is not due until November, the governor said.
His position remained unchanged. "My goal ultimately would be to get rid of it but not in this year's budget."

Adding up the tax cuts already put in place by the Pataki Administration to the new package he has put forward would slice a huge $6.3 billion from the state's revenues in fiscal 1998, a sum that would grow to $7.7 billion by fiscal 2000, the Moody's analyst calculated.

"The array of popular tax cut proposals cannot all be accommodated in the current financial plan, and difficult spending reductions in the areas of Medicaid and higher education will be necessary to balance the budget," Kurtter added, predicting the state's budget was unlikely to be approved by April 1, when it is due, as a result.

Other major initiatives, such as Pataki's welfare plan, which is needed to bring the state's program in compliance with federal rules approved in August, have yet to move beyond preliminary staff discussions, the governor said.
A plan for a new borrowing arm for New York City still is being thrashed out, though last week city sources had been optimistic an agreement could be reached as soon as this week.

"There are serious negotiations underway on a number of the issues and we're pretty close we think on the Infrastructure Finance Authority, the New York City Infrastructure Finance Bill, and some of the others, but on the welfare proposal, not at this point," Pataki said.
